narration: Say an on-call engineer ships a routine change.
A made-up online store stops taking orders.
beats.visual_intent: the engineer at a laptop late at night presses deploy; beside them the store's order counter slows and flatlines

grounding.claim: the engineer, the change and the online store are an invented incident

narration: Next morning, the post-mortem opens.
Every head in the room
turns to the engineer.
beats.visual_intent: the meeting room drawn from above; one by one every head swivels until all of them point at the engineer, then the frame holds on that moment

grounding.claim: the meeting and the room's reaction are part of the invented incident

narration: You have been in that room.
Here are three steps
that turn it toward the system instead.
beats.visual_intent: the presenter, beside a small sketch of the room, promises three steps; the words toward the system settle under them

narration: So why do the heads turn?
Finding the culprit feels like accountability.
Watch what it costs.
beats.visual_intent: the frozen room from the hook, with the word accountability hovering over the engineer and a question mark beside it

grounding.claim: blaming has a cost for what the team learns, shown in the next beats

narration: The engineer knows what the deploy screen showed,
and what they tried first.
With every head turned,
less of it gets said.
beats.visual_intent: the engineer's thought bubble holds two sketches, the deploy screen and the first thing they tried; as the heads stay turned the bubble shrinks and fades, unsaid

grounding.claim: the people closest to an incident usually hold the most useful information
expecting blame makes people share less
what the engineer saw and tried is invented detail

narration: When you expect blame, you share less.
Problems stay hidden,
and the team learns less.
beats.visual_intent: a short left to right chain of three linked boxes, each arriving as it is said

grounding.claim: people who expect blame tend to share less, so problems stay hidden and the team learns less

narration: A blameless post-mortem examines the system,
the conditions and the decisions,
without punishing the people involved.
beats.visual_intent: the term large at the top; beneath it three targets light in turn, the system, the conditions, the decisions, while a small figure of a person stays unmarked

grounding.claim: a blameless post-mortem examines the system, conditions and decisions without assigning fault or punishing individuals

beats.misconception: blameless means nobody is accountable for anything
narration: Here is where it slips.
Blameless does not mean nobody owns anything.
The engineer still gives a full account.
The team still owns the fixes.
beats.visual_intent: a split card: on one side the two things that stay, full account and owns the fixes, drawn firmly and ticked

grounding.claim: blameless is not the absence of accountability: people give a full account and the team owns the fixes

narration: What goes is punishment for an honest mistake.
Reckless acts?
Those go elsewhere.
beats.visual_intent: the other half of the split card: punishment for an honest mistake is struck through; a small side note for reckless acts points out of the room

grounding.claim: what is removed is punishment for honest mistakes
reckless or malicious acts are handled through other processes, not the post-mortem

recall.prompt: remember what the room lost when every head turned?

narration: Remember that fading bubble?
Step one gets it back.
Before anyone discusses the incident,
the lead says what the meeting is for.
To learn and fix the system, not to blame.
beats.visual_intent: the faded thought bubble returns small in the corner; the team lead writes the ground rule as a header across the whiteboard, where it stays for the rest of the meeting

grounding.claim: the person closest to the incident holds the most useful information
stating at the start that the meeting is for learning and improving the system, not blame, is common practice
the team lead's words are an invented example

narration: Step two, you rebuild the night in order,
as each person saw it then.
beats.visual_intent: a timeline draws itself left to right under the header, with empty moment markers spaced along the night

grounding.claim: a useful review rebuilds the sequence in order, recording what each person knew and could see then

narration: The change passed code review.
Staging looked green.
The engineer's phone showed no alert.
Each move made sense.
beats.visual_intent: the timeline fills: at each moment a small screen shows only what that person could see then, review passed, staging green, a phone with no alert

grounding.claim: the review, staging and alert details are the invented incident's conditions
actions usually made sense given what people could see at the time

beats.misconception: once you know how it ended, the mistake was obvious and they should have seen it
narration: It looks obvious now.
It was not on anyone's screen then.
That pull is hindsight bias,
and a bad ending makes people look worse.
So you ask why each move made sense.
beats.visual_intent: the hindsight answer hovers in grey above the timeline; it drops toward each small screen in turn and is on none of them; the term hindsight bias is written beside it

grounding.claim: once the outcome is known it seems more predictable than it was
a bad outcome makes earlier decisions and people look worse
investigate why an action looked reasonable at the time

narration: So, you say the rule.
Then you rebuild it as they saw it.
on_screen: Rebuild it as they saw it
beats.visual_intent: two short step cards side by side, the first two of three slots filled

grounding.claim: state the purpose at the start
rebuild the timeline as people saw it then

narration: Then the manager asks,
why did you ship without checking?
That is the first blaming remark.
The lead's answer matters as much as the rule.
on_screen: Why did you ship without checking?
beats.visual_intent: the manager's why question appears in a speech bubble; the engineer's small thought bubble begins to shrink again while the lead turns toward the manager

grounding.claim: the manager's question is part of the invented meeting
how blame-like remarks are handled matters as much as setting the rule
why-did-you questions put people on the defensive

narration: Here is the rewrite.
What did the deploy screen show you?
One question gets a name.
The other gets something to fix.
on_screen: What did the deploy screen show you?
beats.visual_intent: the why question is crossed out and the what question is written beside it; under each, what it gets you, a name or something to fix

grounding.claim: what and how questions draw out more detail than who or why-did-you questions

narration: Your turn. Who approved this?
Rewrite it in your head.
beats.visual_intent: a second who question appears in a speech bubble with an empty space beside it for the viewer's rewrite

grounding.claim: who questions can be rewritten as what and how questions

narration: Maybe, how did the change get through?
Keep asking what made it easy to do,
and hard to catch.
on_screen: How did the change get through?
beats.visual_intent: the who question is crossed out and the how question written beside it; then the through-line question is written large across the board, and everything slows

grounding.claim: how did the change get through is a what and how question
the useful question is what in the system made the action easy to take and hard to catch

beats.misconception: the finding is that the engineer made a mistake; human error is the cause, and the case is closed
narration: Stop at the engineer, and you have human error.
It explains little.
Keep asking, and conditions appear.
beats.visual_intent: a single arrow runs from the failed checkout straight to the engineer, labelled human error; then it is erased

grounding.claim: stopping at human error explains little

narration: The checkout path had no automated test.
Staging lacked production's payment setting.
The failed-order alert went to an unwatched dashboard.
Several conditions. Do not stop at the first.
beats.visual_intent: three arrows grow in from different parts of the system, each as it is named, and converge on the failed checkout; the words several conditions settle under them

grounding.claim: the three conditions are the invented incident's system details
incidents usually arise from several contributing conditions combining; do not stop at the first cause found

recall.question: Which finding still lands on the engineer?
options: A: no automated test on checkout
B: root cause, a deploy step was missed
C: alert went to an unwatched dashboard
recall.why: B names nobody, but a missed step is a human-error finding about the person who deployed; its only fix is be more careful
recall.tempting_wrong: none of them, because nobody is named

narration: Three findings from our meeting.
A, no automated test on checkout.
B, root cause, a deploy step was missed.
C, the alert went to an unwatched dashboard.
Which still lands on the engineer?
Pause, and decide.
on_screen: Which finding still lands on the engineer?
A: no automated test on checkout
B: root cause, a deploy step was missed
C: alert went to an unwatched dashboard
beats.visual_intent: the question and three finding cards as peers, then a real silent pause

grounding.claim: findings can name a system condition or stop at a person
stopping at human error explains little
the three findings are drawn from the invented incident

narration: It is B. It names nobody,
but its only fix is, be more careful.
No name is not the same as no blame.
A and C point at the system.
on_screen: no name is not no blame
beats.visual_intent: card B is marked with its only fix, be more careful; then cards A and C glow as system conditions while B stays grey

grounding.claim: stopping at human error explains little
be more careful fixes rarely stop recurrence, because the conditions remain
A and C name contributing conditions in the system

beats.misconception: the fix is to tell people to be more careful, or to retrain or remove the person
narration: So your action card cannot say, be more careful.
Every condition would still be standing.
Training can help, but never alone.
beats.visual_intent: the action-item card reads be more careful, with the three conditions from the arrows still standing beside it; then it is struck through

grounding.claim: fixes that only ask people to be more careful rarely stop recurrence, because the conditions remain
training can be part of a fix, but on its own leaves the conditions in place

narration: Change the system instead.
Add a checkout test.
Match the staging setting.
Route the alert to whoever is on call.
beats.visual_intent: three system changes replace the struck-through card, one per condition, each arriving as it is said

grounding.claim: good action items change tools, checks, defaults or procedures
the three fixes answer the invented conditions

narration: You give each fix a named owner,
and you track it to done.
beats.visual_intent: each of the three fixes gains an owner tag, then its checkbox ticks to done, one after another

grounding.claim: each action item needs a named owner and tracking until done

recall.prompt: say the three steps to yourself, against an incident you remember

narration: Now pick an incident you remember.
Before I say them,
run the three steps yourself.
beats.visual_intent: a blank three-step card for the viewer's own incident, its slots empty during a short quiet gap

narration: The rule. The timeline as they saw it.
What made it easy.
And one fix, with its owner.
on_screen: The timeline as they saw it
beats.visual_intent: the three slots fill one at a time, then one fix line with an owner tag appears at the bottom of the card

grounding.claim: state the purpose first
rebuild what each person could see
ask what made the action easy to take
every fix needs an owner

narration: Same room. Same engineer.
Now every head faces the board,
where each fix has an owner.
beats.visual_intent: the meeting room from the hook, drawn from above; every head swivels from the engineer to the board, where the three converging conditions each carry an owned, ticked fix

grounding.claim: the meeting is the invented incident again
system fixes each need an owner

narration: Not who slipped,
but what made the slip easy,
and hard to catch.
beats.visual_intent: the presenter closes, level and firm, beside the pocket rule

grounding.claim: the useful question is what made the action easy to take and hard to catch
